expectedText:
CALIFORNIA FREELANCE WORKER PROTECTION ACT AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme Corp. · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE AND COVERAGE
Acme Corp. ("Hiring Party") is engaging Jordan Lee ("Freelance Worker") to provide the following professional services in exchange for $2,500: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. This agreement is intended to satisfy the written-contract requirements of California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, Business and Professions Code § 18100 et seq.

WHO AND WHAT THIS LAW COVERS
California's Freelance Worker Protection Act (Business and Professions Code § 18100 et seq., added by SB 988 and effective January 1, 2025) applies to a contract between a "hiring party" and a "freelance worker" for "professional services" worth $250 or more. A "freelance worker" is a person, or an organization made up of no more than one person, hired as a bona fide independent contractor to provide professional services for an amount that reaches $250 either in a single contract or when several contracts between the same hiring party and worker are added together over the immediately preceding 120 days. A "hiring party" is any person or organization in California that retains a freelance worker for professional services, except the United States government, the State of California or its subdivisions, a foreign government, or an individual hiring services for the personal benefit of themselves, their family members, or their homestead. "Professional services" is defined by cross-reference to a separate Labor Code statute, which lists specific categories of work — including marketing, graphic design, freelance writing, editing, and still photography, among others — several of which carry their own additional conditions. The Act applies only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Freelance worker” means a person or organization composed of no more than one person, whether or not incorporated or employing a trade name, that is hired or retained as a bona fide independent contractor by a hiring party to provide professional services in exchange for an amount equal to or greater than two hundred and fifty dollars ($250), either by itself or when aggregated with all contracts for services between the same hiring party and independent contractor during the immediately preceding 120 days."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18101.)
  "“Hiring party” means a person or organization in the State of California that retains a freelance worker to provide professional services, except any of the following: (1) The United States government. (2) The State of California or any subdivision thereof. (3) A foreign government. (4) An individual hiring services for the personal benefit of themselves, their family members, or their homestead."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18101.)
  "“Professional services” has the same meaning as paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2778 of the Labor Code."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18101.)
  "“Professional services” means services that meet any of the following: (A) Marketing, provided that the contracted work is original and creative in character and the result of which depends primarily on the invention, imagination, or talent of the individual or work that is an essential part of or necessarily incident to any of the contracted work."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2778(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2778.)
  "This part applies only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18107 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18107.)
  Known gap: The three citations to Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101 (subdivisions (a), (b), and (c)) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent corroborating sources for one another. The citation to Labor Code § 2778(b)(2) is an independent section that § 18101(c) incorporates by cross-reference for the definition of "professional services"; that Labor Code definition was itself amended by AB 1514 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 305, Sec. 1), effective January 1, 2026, and the quote here reflects the current, post-amendment text as verified on 2026-09-04. This clause does not reproduce the full list of occupation-specific categories in Labor Code § 2778(b)(2), nor the further conditions attached to several of them (e.g., photographers, translators, licensed estheticians); whether a specific engagement falls within that list is not determined here. The citation to Bus. & Prof. Code § 18107 is an independent section confirming the January 1, 2025 applicability date; it does not address retroactive application to contracts predating that date.

WRITTEN-CONTRACT REQUIREMENT
Whenever a hiring party retains a freelance worker under California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, the contract between them must be in writing. The hiring party must furnish the freelance worker a signed copy of that written contract, either physically or electronically, and must retain the contract for at least four years. A hiring party's refusal to provide a written contract does not by itself defeat a freelance worker's other legal remedies: the law states that a freelance worker may still enforce an oral contract or recover under the doctrine of promissory estoppel, and specific facts — a rate representation by the hiring party, a written summary of the rate and work the freelance worker provided before starting, or the freelance worker's performance of the work as understood — may serve as evidence that a contract was formed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Whenever a hiring party retains the services of a freelance worker, the contract between the hiring party and the freelance worker shall be in writing. The hiring party shall furnish a signed copy of the written contract, either physically or electronically, to the freelance worker. The hiring party shall retain the contract for no less than four years."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18103.)
  "This section does not limit existing contract law, including, but not limited to, that it does not prevent a freelance worker from enforcing an oral contract or recovering under the doctrine of promissory estoppel. Notwithstanding a refusal by the hiring party to provide a written contract as required by subdivision (a), the following may be evidence that a contract was formed between the parties: (1) The hiring party made representations to the freelance worker regarding the rate for services to be performed. (2) The freelance worker provided in writing any document to the hiring party, including email, text message, or other electronic communication, a summary of the rate and work to be performed prior to performing the work. (3) The freelance worker performed the work that the freelance worker understood was to be performed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18103.)
  Known gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103 (subdivisions (a) and (c)), and are not independent sources for one another. This clause does not cover subdivision (b)'s list of required contract contents, addressed in a separate clause, nor the statutory damages that attach to a hiring party's refusal to provide a written contract, addressed in the enforcement clause. It also does not resolve, for a specific dispute, whether an oral agreement or the listed forms of evidence would in fact establish that a contract was formed — that determination is fact-specific and not made here.

MINIMUM CONTRACT CONTENTS
The written contract required by California's Freelance Worker Protection Act must include, at minimum, four items: the name and mailing address of each party; an itemized list of all services to be provided by the freelance worker, including the value of those services and the rate and method of compensation; the date on which the hiring party will pay the contracted compensation, or the mechanism by which that date will be determined; and the date by which the freelance worker must submit a list of services rendered, to meet the hiring party's internal processing deadlines for timely payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The contract shall include, at minimum, all of the following information: (1) The name and mailing address of each party. (2) An itemized list of all services to be provided by the freelance worker, including the value of those services and the rate and method of compensation. (3) The date on which the hiring party shall pay the contracted compensation or the mechanism by which the date shall be determined. (4) The date by which a freelance worker shall submit a list of services rendered under the contract to the hiring party to meet the hiring party’s internal processing deadlines for purposes of timely payment of compensation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18103.)
  Known gap: This citation is a single subdivision, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(b), of the same section covered in the written-contract-requirement clause (subdivisions (a) and (c)) — it is not an independent corroborating source. This clause states only the four statutory minimums; it does not address what additional terms a contract may contain beyond these required items, nor how specific or detailed the required itemization must be to satisfy the statute, which the text does not further define.

TIMELY-PAYMENT RULE
Under California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, a hiring party must pay a freelance worker the compensation specified in their contract on or before the date the contract specifies as due; if the contract does not specify a due date, payment is due no later than 30 days after the freelance worker completes the contracted services. Once a freelance worker has begun performing services under a contract, the hiring party may not condition timely payment on the freelance worker accepting less compensation than the contract specifies, or on the freelance worker providing more goods or services, or granting more intellectual property rights, than the contract calls for.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided by law, a hiring party shall pay a freelance worker the compensation specified by a contract for professional services: (1) On or before the date compensation is due pursuant to the contract. (2) If the contract does not specify when the hiring party shall pay, no later than 30 days after the completion of the freelance worker’s services under the contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18102.)
  "Once a freelance worker has commenced performance of services under a contract, a hiring party shall not require as a condition of timely payment that the freelance worker do either of the following: (1) Accept less compensation than the amount of compensation specified by the contract. (2) Provide more goods or services or grant more intellectual property rights than agreed to in the contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18102.)
  Known gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102 (subdivisions (a) and (b)), and are not independent sources for one another. This clause states the payment-timing default and the anti-lowball protection; it does not cover the remedies for a late or refused payment, which are addressed in the enforcement clause, and it does not address the separate written-contract or contract-contents requirements covered in other clauses.

ANTI-RETALIATION PROTECTION AND NON-WAIVABILITY
California's Freelance Worker Protection Act prohibits a hiring party from discriminating against, or taking any adverse action against, a freelance worker that penalizes the freelance worker for, or is reasonably likely to deter the freelance worker from: opposing a practice the Act prohibits; participating in a proceeding to enforce the Act; seeking to enforce rights the Act provides; or otherwise asserting or attempting to assert those rights. The Act separately states that any waiver of its protections is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A hiring party shall not discriminate or take any adverse action against a freelance worker that penalizes a freelance worker for, or is reasonably likely to deter a freelance worker from, taking any of the following actions: (a) Opposing any practice prohibited by this part. (b) Participating in proceedings related to the enforcement of this part. (c) Seeking to enforce rights provided by this part. (d) Otherwise asserting or attempting to assert rights provided by this part."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18105 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18105.)
  "A waiver of any provision in this part shall be deemed contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18104 (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18104.)
  Known gap: Bus. & Prof. Code § 18105 and § 18104 are independent sections of the Act, not subdivisions of a single section — each addresses a different protection (anti-retaliation and non-waivability, respectively) rather than corroborating the other. This clause does not further define what specifically counts as an "adverse action" beyond the statute's own list of protected activities, which the Act does not itself elaborate on, nor does it address the civil remedies available for a retaliation violation, which are addressed generally in the enforcement clause.

ENFORCEMENT AND REMEDIES
An aggrieved freelance worker, or a public prosecutor, may bring a civil action to enforce California's Freelance Worker Protection Act. A prevailing plaintiff is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and costs, injunctive relief, and any other remedies the court deems appropriate. The statute sets three specific damages measures: if a freelance worker requested a written contract before starting work and the hiring party refused to provide one, the freelance worker is entitled to an additional $1,000; if the hiring party failed to pay by the time the Act requires, the freelance worker is entitled to damages of up to twice the amount that remained unpaid when payment was due; and for any other violation of the Act, the freelance worker may be awarded damages equal to the value of the contract or of the work performed, whichever is greater.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An aggrieved freelance worker or a public prosecutor may bring a civil action to enforce this part."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18106.)
  "A prevailing plaintiff in an action alleging a violation of this part is entitled to reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, injunctive relief, and any other remedies deemed appropriate by the court. Damages shall be awarded to an aggrieved freelance worker as follows: (1) If the freelance worker requested a written contact prior to commencing work under the contract and the hiring party refused in violation of Section 18103, the freelance worker shall be awarded an additional one thousand dollars ($1,000). (2) If the hiring party failed to pay the freelance worker the contracted compensation by the time required under Section 18102, the freelance worker shall be awarded damages up to twice the amount that remained unpaid at the time payment was due. If the freelance worker requested a written contract prior to commencing work under the contract and the hiring party refused in violation of Section 18103, the amount unpaid shall be determined by the rate the freelance worker reasonably understood to apply to the work. (3) If the hiring party violates any other provision of this part, the freelance worker may be awarded damages equal to the value of the contract or the work performed, whichever is greater."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Business and Professions Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=18106.)
  Known gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106 (subdivisions (a) and (b)), and are not independent sources for one another. Note: the enacted, codified text of § 18106(b)(1) reads "requested a written contact" (not "contract") while the parallel phrase in § 18106(b)(2) reads "requested a written contract" — this inconsistency was verified as present in the official statutory text itself (confirmed identical across two independent fetches with different browser user-agent strings) and is not a transcription error introduced here. This clause does not cover who qualifies as a "public prosecutor" (defined in Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(d) by cross-reference to Labor Code § 180, not independently verified for this clause set) or the procedural mechanics of bringing such an action.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
